title: Reverse Integer
description:
Given a signed 32-bit integer `x`, reverse its decimal digits and return the result. The sign stays with the number.

If the reversed value does not fit in a signed 32-bit integer (`[-2^31, 2^31 - 1]`), return `0`. Assume you may **not** use 64-bit integers to detect the overflow; check before each multiply-and-add.
hints: Peel digits off with x % 10 and x // 10, building the result as result * 10 + digit. Work on the absolute value and reapply the sign.
Before computing result * 10 + digit, check whether it would exceed 2^31 - 1: result > 214748364, or result == 214748364 and digit > 7 (digit > 8 for the negative side).
In Python you can simply compare the final value against the bounds, but be ready to explain the pre-check an interviewer expects in C++ or Java.
approach:
**Key insight: build the reversed number one digit at a time with `rev = rev * 10 + digit`, and detect overflow *before* performing that step by comparing `rev` with `INT_MAX // 10`.**

Strip the sign and work on `|x|`. Each iteration takes the last digit with `divmod(x, 10)`. Before appending it, overflow happens if `rev > 214748364`, or if `rev == 214748364` and the digit would push past the last digit of the limit: `7` for positive results (`2147483647`), `8` for negative ones (`-2147483648`). Finally reapply the sign.

**Why the pre-check suffices:** if `rev < 214748364`, then `rev * 10 + 9 <= 2147483639`, safely in range. If `rev > 214748364`, then `rev * 10 >= 2147483650`, already out of range. Only the boundary value needs the digit comparison. In fact, when `rev == 214748364` the input had 10 digits and started with 1 or 2, so the final digit is at most 2 and the equality branch never fires for valid 32-bit inputs; keeping it makes the reasoning complete.

**Python note:** unbounded ints mean `int(str(abs(x))[::-1])` plus a range check also works. Interviewers at Apple and Microsoft usually ask for the arithmetic version and the overflow argument, because that is the point of the question.

**Common mistakes:** checking the range after the multiplication (undefined behaviour in C++, silent wraparound in Java); forgetting that `-2^31` cannot be negated in 32 bits (handle the sign separately); mishandling trailing zeros (they vanish naturally with the arithmetic approach).

**Interview follow-ups:** (1) String to Integer (atoi) uses the same pre-multiplication overflow check. (2) Palindrome Number: reverse only half the digits. (3) Reverse the bits instead of the decimal digits (Reverse Bits).
